Early Blight.overview: Early blight is a common fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It primarily affects older foliage first, producing dark brown target-like circular spots with concentric rings, surrounded by yellow chlorotic halos.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings ('target board' pattern)
Yellowing of foliage surrounding the lesions
Starts on lower older leaves and progresses upward
Severe infection leads to leaf death, defoliation, and sunscald on fruits
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds and healthy seedlings
Practice 2-3 year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops (potato, brinjal, chilli)
Ensure adequate plant spacing (60 x 45 cm) for optimal canopy aeration
Use drip irrigation or furrow irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers
non_chemical_control: Remove and safely burn or bury infected lower leaves as soon as noticed
Apply organic mulch (straw or plastic) to prevent soil splash onto lower leaves
Foliar spray with Trichoderma viride or Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 5 g/litre
verified_treatment: Spray Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2 g/L at the first sign of disease
In severe cases, spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L
Repeat application after 10-14 days if wet, humid weather persists
safety_precautions: Wear protective gloves, eye goggles, and a face mask during chemical spraying
Observe a mandatory Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI) of 7-10 days after spraying
Avoid spraying during high winds or midday peak sunshine

Late Blight.overview: Late blight is a destructive oomycete disease caused by Phytophthora infestans. It develops rapidly under cool, wet, and high humidity conditions, causing water-soaked pale lesions that turn dark brown and rot rapidly.
symptoms: Water-soaked, dark olive to brown lesions on leaves and stems
White velvety fungal growth on the underside of leaves during humid conditions
Rapid collapse and browning of foliage resembling frost injury
Firm, greasy dark brown lesions on green or ripe fruits
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant tomato varieties
Destroy cull piles and volunteer tomato and potato plants in the vicinity
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation and reduce canopy wetness duration
non_chemical_control: Immediately prune and bury heavily blighted branches
Ensure wide spacing and good air drainage in low-lying field spots
Spray with copper oxychloride formulations before rain periods
verified_treatment: Prophylactic spray: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 3 g/L
Curative spray on disease onset: Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2 g/L
safety_precautions: Never wash spray equipment in drinking water sources or ponds
Adhere to a 7-day pre-harvest interval before harvesting tomatoes
Late Blight.source_url: ICAR-IIHR (Indian Institute of Horticultural Research) Tomato Disease Compendium

Bacterial Spot.overview: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria. It leads to small water-soaked dark spots on leaves and scabby lesions on fruits, exacerbated by warm, rainy weather.
symptoms: Small, circular to angular water-soaked dark spots on leaves
Lesions turn brown to black with a narrow yellow margin
Scabby, elevated spots with dark borders on tomato fruits
Severe leaf spot coalesces causing shot-hole appearance and defoliation
prevention: Use certified disease-free treated seed (hot water treatment at 50°C for 25 minutes)
Avoid working in field rows when plants are wet with dew or rain
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops for at least 2 years
non_chemical_control: Remove crop residues after harvest through deep summer plowing
Spray Pseudomonas fluorescens (biocontrol agent) @ 5 g/L
verified_treatment: Foliar spray with Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L mixed with Streptocycline @ 0.1 g/L (100 ppm) at 10-15 day intervals
safety_precautions: Use protective gear during preparation and application of antibiotic/copper mixtures

Yellow Leaf Curl Virus.overview: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is a begomovirus transmitted by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). It causes severe stunting, upward leaf curling, yellowing, and drastic flower drop.
symptoms: Marked upward curling and cup-shaped crinkling of leaf margins
Interveinal chlorosis and yellowing of young leaves
Severely stunted plant height with bunched terminal shoots
Premature drop of blossoms, resulting in negligible fruit setting
prevention: Install yellow sticky traps @ 12-15 traps per acre to monitor and reduce whiteflies
Grow barrier crops like maize, sorghum, or pearl millet (4 rows around the border)
Use 40-mesh insect-proof nylon nets in nursery beds
non_chemical_control: Rogue out and destroy virus-infected plants during early vegetative stage
Spray Neem Oil (Azadirachtin 1500 ppm) @ 3-5 ml/L to deter whitefly vectors
verified_treatment: Vector management: Spray Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.3 ml/L or Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1 ml/L
safety_precautions: Do not spray systemic neonicotinoids during peak pollinator visitation hours
Yellow Leaf Curl Virus.source_url: ICAR-Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR) Pest Advisory

Leaf Mold.overview: Leaf mold is caused by the fungus Passalora fulva (formerly Cladosporium fulvum). It is especially prevalent in greenhouses and high-humidity humid conditions.
symptoms: Pale greenish-yellow chlorotic spots on upper leaf surfaces
Olive-green to grayish-brown velvety mold on the underside of corresponding spots
Leaves wither, curl, and die prematurely from bottom to top
prevention: Maximize greenhouse ventilation and reduce relative humidity below 85%
Increase plant spacing to promote sunlight penetration and air movement
Avoid wetting tomato leaves during irrigation
non_chemical_control: Prune lower suckers and dense canopy foliage
Biological control: Trichoderma harzianum foliar spray @ 5 g/L
verified_treatment: Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2 g/L or Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2 g/L
safety_precautions: Ensure well-ventilated conditions when handling chemical fungicides

Healthy.overview: The leaf appears vigorous, green, and devoid of significant pathological lesions or fungal/bacterial blight.
symptoms: Uniform green color across leaf surface and veins
No chlorotic yellowing, necrotic spots, or curling observed
Firm leaf texture with healthy turgor pressure
prevention: Continue balanced N-P-K fertilization according to crop growth stage
Maintain routine weekly visual scouting for early pest or disease signs
Ensure consistent soil moisture without waterlogging
non_chemical_control: Routine prophylactic spraying of cow dung-urine slurry or neem cake extract
Beneficial companion planting with marigolds to deter root-knot nematodes
verified_treatment: No chemical intervention required for healthy plants
safety_precautions: Avoid unnecessary pesticide sprays to protect natural predators and bees
Healthy.source_url: ICAR Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) for Solanaceous Vegetables

Curl Virus.overview: Chilli leaf curl disease is caused by Chilli Leaf Curl Begomovirus and vectored by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). Often co-occurring with thrips and mite feeding which causes upward or downward curling.
symptoms: Upward curling, puckering, and crinkling of leaves
Reduction in leaf size, thickening and shortening of internodes
Crowded, bushy stunted appearance of plants
Drastic reduction in flowering and small, malformed fruits
prevention: Grow barrier crops like maize or pearl millet (3-4 rows) around the plot
Use silver/black reflective plastic mulch to repel whitefly and thrips vectors
Install yellow sticky traps (15/acre) and blue sticky traps (10/acre)
non_chemical_control: Rogue and burn symptomatic plants immediately during early stages
Foliar spray of 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) or Azadirachtin 10,000 ppm @ 1 ml/L
verified_treatment: Vector control: Spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.2 g/L or Fipronil 5% SC @ 1.5 ml/L
For whiteflies specifically: Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.2 g/L or Pyriproxyfen 10% EC @ 1 ml/L
safety_precautions: Do not apply chemicals in bloom period; observe 7-day harvest waiting period
Curl Virus.source_url: ICAR-Indian Institute of Spices Research (IISR) & TNAU Agritech

Bacterial Spot.overview: Caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria. Promoted by high temperature (24-30°C) and frequent rainfall.
symptoms: Circular to irregular dark brown spots with a greasy water-soaked appearance
Spots on leaves may coalesce, causing yellowing and premature leaf fall
Small, blister-like raised rough spots on green chilli pods
prevention: Seed treatment with hot water (50°C for 25 mins) or Streptocycline @ 100 ppm
Avoid overhead irrigation and field entry when plants are wet
non_chemical_control: Spray Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 5 g/litre at 15-day intervals
Remove and destroy crop debris immediately after harvest
verified_treatment: Spray Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L + Streptocycline @ 0.1 g/L twice at 10-day intervals
safety_precautions: Use safety mask and gloves when handling bactericides
Bacterial Spot.source_url: ICAR-IISR Chilli Integrated Pest & Disease Management

Cercospora Leaf Spot.overview: Caused by Cercospora capsici, also known as 'frogeye leaf spot'. Highly prevalent in humid tropical conditions.
symptoms: Circular lesions with whitish or grayish centers and distinct dark brown margins ('frogeye' appearance)
Lesions enlarge up to 1 cm and may develop yellow halos
Severely affected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely, exposing chilli fruit to sun scald
prevention: Practice crop rotation avoiding solanaceous crops for 2 seasons
Maintain adequate spacing between rows to enhance air flow
non_chemical_control: Collect and destroy fallen infected leaves from the soil surface
Apply organic bio-agent Trichoderma viride @ 5 g/L
verified_treatment: Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1 g/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1 ml/L
safety_precautions: Observe recommended pre-harvest interval before plucking green chillies

Healthy Leaf.overview: The chilli foliage exhibits normal healthy coloration, intact leaf margins, and absence of fungal or viral lesions.
symptoms: Dark green, glossy leaf surface
No curling, mottling, or spot lesions
prevention: Maintain balanced soil fertilization (N:P:K 120:60:60 kg/ha in splits)
Scout weekly for thrips or mite activity underneath tender leaves
non_chemical_control: Preventive foliar application of bio-stimulants or diluted panchagavya @ 3%
verified_treatment: No chemical fungicide or bactericide necessary

Cercospora Spot.overview: Cercospora melongenae produces circular to irregular leaf spots leading to premature defoliation in eggplant.
symptoms: Circular brown spots with concentric rings and chlorotic borders
Spots may drop out, leaving a ragged shot-hole effect
Premature leaf drop leading to reduced fruit size and yield
prevention: Deep summer ploughing to bury overwintering fungal spores
Maintain 75 x 60 cm spacing for good air circulation
non_chemical_control: Prompt sanitation: destroy infected lower leaf prunings
Spray Trichoderma viride @ 5 g/L as a protective canopy bio-spray
verified_treatment: Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2 g/L or Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1 g/L at 10-14 day intervals
safety_precautions: Wear personal protective equipment; adhere to 5-day PHI

Begomovirus.overview: Whitefly-transmitted virus causing severe leaf deformation, stunted plants, and poor fruit development.
symptoms: Yellow mosaic patterns on leaves with vein thickening
Bushy, stunted growth with small leathery leaves
Flowering is severely curtailed and fruit set is negligible
prevention: Install 15 yellow sticky traps per acre across the field
Use nursery insect-proof netting to raise disease-free saplings
non_chemical_control: Uproot and destroy infected plants at early detection
Spray neem oil 10,000 ppm @ 2 ml/L to deter vector feeding
verified_treatment: Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.3 ml/L for whitefly control
safety_precautions: Avoid spraying during active bee foraging hours

Healthy.overview: Vigorous brinjal foliage with broad, healthy leaves without spot or virus symptoms.
symptoms: Normal broad green leaves with regular pubescence
No chlorotic mottling or fungal lesions
prevention: Provide regular irrigation and balanced NPK top dressings
non_chemical_control: Prophylactic foliar spray of neem oil or seaweed extract
verified_treatment: No chemical intervention needed

Leaf Curl Virus.overview: A serious viral disease transmitted by the whitefly vector (Bemisia tabaci), often grouped with Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus (YVMV).
symptoms: Vein clearing on tender young leaves
Upward curling, thickening and yellow network of veins
Leaves become leathery and crinkled with stunted growth
Fruits turn yellowish-white, fibrous, and unmarketable
prevention: Sow YVMV-tolerant/resistant okra varieties (e.g., Parbhani Kranti, Arka Anamika)
Grow 3 border rows of maize or sorghum to trap incoming whiteflies
non_chemical_control: Strict roguing of affected plants within the first 30-45 days
Foliar spray of 5% NSKE (Neem Seed Kernel Extract)
verified_treatment: Vector control: Seed treatment with Imidacloprid 70% WS @ 5 g/kg seed; foliar spray of Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.35 g/L
safety_precautions: Maintain 5-day pre-harvest waiting period before picking tender okra pods

Cercospora Leaf Spot.overview: Caused by Cercospora abelmoschi and Cercospora malayensis. Manifests in warm, humid weather.
symptoms: Brown to grayish circular or irregular spots on leaves
Spots merge causing extensive blighting of the leaf blade
Severe defoliation affects fruit quality and yield
prevention: Maintain proper plant spacing (60 x 30 cm)
Avoid prolonged wet foliage
non_chemical_control: Collect and burn fallen leaves
Spray bio-agent Trichoderma viride @ 5 g/L
verified_treatment: Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2 g/L or Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1 g/L
safety_precautions: Always observe mandatory safety intervals before pod harvesting

Healthy.overview: Normal, healthy okra leaf displaying deep green palmately lobed morphology with no chlorosis or necrosis.
symptoms: Uniform green color across lobes
Absence of vein clearing or necrotic lesions
prevention: Maintain regular weeding and moisture control
non_chemical_control: Apply vermicompost and neem cake to soil
verified_treatment: No treatment required

Powdery Mildew.overview: Caused by Podosphaera xanthii (or Erysiphe cichoracearum). Characterized by conspicuous white talcum-like powdery fungal patches on leaf surfaces.
symptoms: White, talcum-powder-like circular spots on upper and lower leaf surfaces
Spots enlarge and coalesce to cover the entire leaf blade and petioles
Infected leaves turn yellow, then brown, and become dry and brittle
Premature leaf loss exposes cucumbers to sunscald
prevention: Plant resistant cucumber cultivars where available
Ensure full sunlight exposure and open trellis training for airflow
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer which stimulates lush susceptible tissue
non_chemical_control: Foliar spray of dilute baking soda solution (0.5% sodium bicarbonate + 0.1% horticultural oil)
Spray biocontrol Ampelomyces quisqualis or Bacillus subtilis @ 5 g/L
verified_treatment: Spray Wettable Sulphur 80% WP @ 2.5 g/L (avoid if temperature > 32°C)
Or spray Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1 ml/L
safety_precautions: Do not apply sulphur within 14 days of an oil spray to prevent severe phytotoxicity

Downy Mildew.overview: Caused by Pseudoperonospora cubensis. Highly devastating water-mold disease in cool, damp, foggy, or rainy conditions.
symptoms: Angular, pale green to bright yellow spots on the upper leaf surface bounded by leaf veins
Purplish-gray downy/felt-like growth on the lower leaf surface directly under spots during moist mornings
Spots turn dark brown and necrotic, causing scorched appearance
prevention: Trellis vines to keep foliage off moist soil and improve drying
Irrigate in the early morning using drip lines; avoid overhead wetting
non_chemical_control: Remove early affected leaves and dispose of outside the field
Apply copper hydroxide formulations preventatively
verified_treatment: Preventive: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 3 g/L
Curative: Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2 g/L or Metalaxyl-M 4% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L
safety_precautions: Strictly adhere to a 5-7 day pre-harvest interval before picking harvestable cucumbers

Healthy.overview: Vibrant, green angular lobed cucumber leaf showing no signs of downy mildew angular spots or powdery white coating.
symptoms: Clean, uniform green foliage
Absence of yellow angular chlorosis or white powdery growth
prevention: Maintain balanced fertigation and regular vine training on trellises
non_chemical_control: Preventive application of organic mulch around the root zone
verified_treatment: No chemical fungicide needed
